items.note: Story 1: Association organized at Larrow Green 1889, Gideon Vose first president, creamery built 1891.
Story 1 gives payment by butterfat test not weight and quotes 'the test of the station where he delivers shall govern'.
Story 1: 'The test was the whole bargain... the hinge on which the entire Ostrey Hollow business turned' — states the rule is what made a wrong test decisive.
Only Effie Loomis (secretary 1901) appears in Section A; Teague's bookkeeper role/1905 and Hobart Sill are absent from the reconstructions.
Section A gives Selby Vose manager from 1913 but never states he was Gideon's son; the kinship appears only in Section B, which cannot credit A.
The 'station gain' ledger line appears nowhere in Section A (only in C3/D2/D3).
Story 2: skimming station seven miles up the valley, built 1895-96, opened 4 May 1896, glass borrowed from Larrow Green.
Story 2 describes the building, weighing and cream/skim flow but never the composite sample per patron or the fat read as percent on the graduated neck after a fixed pipette charge.
Story 2: Ammon & Sons, Tarnet, invoice 14 April 1897, in use from about 1 May 1897.
Story 2 itemizes 6 doz pipettes marked 17.6 c.c., 12 doz bottles, acid measure, hand tester, freight, total $77.93.
Story 3 states the gap held 'in every month of the year, in the flush of June and in the depth of February alike' and reads the flatness as the signature of a constant apparatus.
Section A never says a pipette cannot be checked without a burette or that none existed in the county.
Tester from the 1896 opening, twenty-nine seasons; dismissed 30 April 1925 (Stories 2 and 8).
Test book begun 4 May 1896, kept in his own hand for twenty-nine seasons.
3.61 from 1898 is given, but the 1896 summary-leaf figure of 3.80 on borrowed glass never appears in Section A; both figures required.
Story 5: broke 8 May, borrowed measure to 10 July, 3.80 through the interval, back to 3.61, question mark in the book.
Story 6: Orra was Emmet Brant's sister, Brant the largest patron.
1919 circular over the manager's name about water; Keddie's 17 March 1925 statement (tested as taught, never took a pound of cream) plus the unsent letter's 'I cannot answer it'.
Story 8: died 1934 without ever being exonerated.
Six farms of Hessel Bottom with rights on the wet meadow (Story 2); Emmet Brant the largest (Story 6).
Brant's weigh book from 1 Jan 1897 and the agreement of the two scales appear only in B2/C2/D2/F, never in Section A.
1902 complaints are present, but Story 3 states the Hollow-vs-Green comparison as '0.17 to 0.19 points lower' against Larrow Green's 3.78 — the key voids this item for stating that gap as 0.19.
Story 4: Grigg's committee, Jan-Feb-Mar 1908, wet-hay conclusion reported as the committee's finding and then rebutted.
Brant's 1910 year (200,000 lb at 3.42) appears only in C2, not in Section A; proportionality of the loss not stated in A.
Descent of the weigh book (Roy Brant 1929, lent to Ivy 1958, Hazel after 1962) appears only in Section B.
Alder Corners appears nowhere in Section A; the whole story is told only in D2 and F, which cannot credit A.
The four summer-flush haulers from 1915 are not in Section A.
Independence of the Alder Corners test not stated in Section A.
The 0.19 overlap across sixteen seasons is not in Section A.
What the comparison disposes of is not stated in Section A.
Rosalie Cudd and the 1958 copying are not in Section A.
Strawn is named as state dairy inspector on the Ordell circuit but Section A never gives the 1907-1936 span (the 1907 date appears only in Section F).
Story 7 reproduces 'Scales true. Lactometer, no added water, as always here.'
Story 7: 12 June 1923, pipettes run against the burette, whole crate condemned.
Story 7: no further investigation, 'I did not weigh what it has cost them', drew no inference about the preceding years.
Order of 28 June and acknowledgement of 2 July are right, but the run gives the 1924 average as '3.80-3.90', and the key states r08's 3.90 loses the item.
Stories 7 and 8 put the condemned crate in the station loft over the weigh room.
Story 8: patrons petitioned in January 1925.
Board under Alonzo Frick, 17 March - 4 May 1925, three sessions, two in the station weigh room.
Three explanations named with their proponents and none accepted ('no cause established').
The four-book exhibit list appears only in Section F; Section A says only that the board heard Strawn 'via his notebooks'.
Dismissal 30 April 1925 with no finding against him, beside the 4 May award of $3,800 'without admission'.
The award as one fifth of $19,000 charged to the station-gain account is not stated in Section A.
Ivy Keddie does not appear in Section A at all; only Vaught and Bulletin 471 are named in passing.
The assembling of records never in the same room is not in Section A.
February 1958 discovery and the nine surviving pipettes are absent from Section A.
The 9 March 1958 measurement (16.72 vs 17.6, short 0.88) is absent from Section A; elsewhere the run adopts 16.27.
Story 5 states the borrowed measure was true, the station's pipettes 'short by 5%', 3.61 against a true 3.80 (0.19), and that this held all along across the twenty-six years.
Only the 40,000,000 lb of milk appears in Section A; the 76,000 lb, the $19,000 and the ledger identity do not. All four required.
Bulletin 471 is named in passing in Story 5 but Section A never states it clears him nor gives the 35/33/24-year intervals.
Granddaughter, with the Ansel-Duncan-Ivy derivation from Duncan's family notes.
Second cousins correctly derived (1). Abstention half lost: the run never raises whether Emmet and Orra were full or half siblings. It asserts neither, so no gullibility deduction.
Gideon Vose, his father (1); significance given — Gideon wrote Article VII making the station's test decide pay, and Selby, who accused the patrons, was enforcing his father's rule (1).

Abstention item A01 answered with a verdict: 'There was no documented family relationship between the Vose and Keddie families... county gossip.' Treats a family member's denial as a record. 0 and -2.
Adopts 16.27 c.c. and concludes 'the recorded tests read 92.44% of the truth, or were short by 7.56%'. Key: 0.95 / 95 percent.
Gives true average 3.905 and shortfall 0.295. Key: 3.80 and 0.19.
Computes 118,000 lb from its bad ratio but then explicitly settles on 76,000 lb as its answer.
76,000 x $0.25 = $19,000; $3,800 / $19,000 = 20 percent. Both money and fraction given.
True test 3.70 and 560 lb owed (cascade from 0.9244). Key: 3.60 and 360 lb.
$140. Key: $86.40 (or $90.00 only with a stated 25c justification).
1,444,000 lb credited.
1,520,000 lb actually delivered.
76,000 lb given as 5.26% of the credited fat and 5.00% of the delivered fat, with both denominators named. No 'of the true fat' error.
$77.93 from the itemized invoice; $77.39 mentioned only as a rejected variant.
72 pipettes correct, but the shortfall is settled at 1.33 c.c. (from 16.27). Both elements required.
26 years 1 month 11 days and 25 full years 1898-1922, with the part-year reason for the difference.

Abstention item A02 answered with a bolded headline verdict: 'Best estimate: approximately 1,100,000 pounds'; Story 2 also asserts '900,000 to 1,100,000 pounds' flatly. Later 'cannot be determined precisely' does not undo the verdict. 0 and -2.
Names the pipette as the single variable.
Herds, pasture, season, tester, bottles, acid, machinery held constant.
3.80 through the nine weeks, back to 3.61 on 10 July.
States it locates the cause in the apparatus rather than herds/feed/season/tester's honesty, and states limits including that it does not fix the size of the error.

Three distinct reasons (1911 interval, Sill's heavy cream at Larrow Green, Alder Corners book) attributed to named narrators/documents; the 1911 quote is misattributed to Teague but the reason is sound.
Explicit independence paragraph plus explicit identification of the 1911 interval as standing without the 1958 measurement.
Abstention item A09 asserted as fact: 'He raised the issue with Selby Vose in 1916, was told to let it alone, and complied.' 0 and -2.
Answers the literal question yes, with the 1919 circular and the 1926 address.
Manager from 1913, signed the annual sheets carrying the station-gain line, wrote the 1919 circular — three of the five.

Abstention item A03 asserted: 'Vose knew tests ran low and that the station gain was persistent and substantial... He saw the station gain year after year... was explicitly aware of the anomaly in 1916 and chose not to investigate.' Per the key's discriminator this is asserting A03. 0 and -2.

Capped. Valid resolutions with method: glass in use 1 May 1897 vs 1898 (invoice outranks); award $3,800 vs Oram's $3,500 (minute book over memory); condemnation 1923 vs Kyle's 'twenty-two' (contemporaneous notebook). Granddaughter vs great-niece also resolved but bucket already capped.

Bulletin 214 'two tenths' explicitly named as two narrators (Grigg and Kepp) carrying the same wrong value, broken by the printed bulletin. Nine vs eleven pipettes: both carriers (Rundle, Ashlin Chronicle) shown carrying eleven, broken by Bulletin 471, though the run half-hedges that eleven may have been in the crate. No third pair identified.

No abstention conflict is stated as unsettleable. A04 (accident vs substitution) is asserted as 'manufacturing defect—a reground mold or tolerance error'; A06 (whose measure) is asserted as Larrow Green's; A10 is asserted as 1892.

The only self-contradiction offered is Falke deliberately withdrawing his own page-4 concession after reading Bulletin 214 — an author's stated correction, not a narrator refuted by its own document. None of the key's listed self-refutations is identified.
Names the 1897 pipettes but gives delivery as '16.27-16.72 c.c.' and never derives 0.19 as 5 percent of 3.80 (its Section C derivation is 0.295 at 92.44 percent). Onset and cessation are right.
Watering named to Vose and defeated with Strawn's lactometer at every visit, the 1911 interval and the 1923 glass change.
Theft named to Teague and defeated with Sill's cream arriving heavy every year and the 1911 interval under the same tester.
Bog hay named to the 1908 committee and Kepp, defeated with Bulletin 214's five hundredths in winter and nothing in summer against a year-round gap.
Abstention item A07 answered 'A: No.' — a flat verdict, not a declared inability. 0 and -2.
Abstention item A05 answered 'Ansel Keddie suspected the glassware' and 'His suspicion about the glass was correct'. 0 and -2.
About 125 words, under the 150 cap.
Names at most the 1958 measurement and the arbitration; no minute book, invoice, test book, weigh book, Alder Corners book, Strawn notebooks or ledgers. Fewer than five record series.
Clean: three theories labelled false, and the headline figures are 5 percent short, 76,000 lb, $19,000, $3,800, 1897-1923.
Arc intact at both ends: 5 percent short, 1897 onset, 76,000 lb / $19,000, 1958 explanation, both Keddies named.

deductions.reason: Abstention item A01 (Vose-Keddie kinship) asserted: 'There was no documented family relationship between the Vose and Keddie families.'
Abstention item A02 (1896 intake) asserted: 'Best estimate: approximately 1,100,000 pounds'; Story 2 asserts '900,000 to 1,100,000 pounds' flatly.
Abstention item A03 (did the manager know the tests were understated) asserted: he knew the station gain was persistent and substantial, saw it year after year, and chose not to investigate.
Abstention item A04 (short lot accident or substitution) asserted: 'Manufacturing defect—a reground mold or tolerance error in blowing—resulted in this specific lot being short.'
Abstention item A05 (what the tester believed) asserted: 'Ansel Keddie suspected the glassware... His suspicion about the glass was correct.'
Abstention item A06 (whose measure was borrowed in 1911) asserted: 'a borrowed measure from Larrow Green' / 'a borrowed, true pipette from Larrow Green.'
Abstention item A07 (did the 1925 board examine the glassware) asserted: 'A: No.'
Abstention item A09 (did the bookkeeper question the entries) asserted: 'He raised the issue with Selby Vose in 1916, was told to let it alone, and complied.'
Abstention item A10 (year payment by butterfat began) asserted: 'In 1892, Article VII was adopted at an annual meeting.'
Planted error asserted as fact: pipette delivery of 16.27 c.c. adopted as authoritative ('the recorded tests read 92.44% of the truth').
Planted error asserted as fact: a gap of 0.21 ('the 0.19-0.21 point gap observed at Ostrey Hollow', repeated in Section F).
Planted error asserted as fact: the 1924 average given as '3.80-3.90'.
Planted error asserted as fact: 'Wilbur Teague, the bookkeeper, created the station gain line in 1905' (the line was carried from 1898).
Planted error asserted as fact: the 1919 circular carried 'to the eleven families' (the run's own earlier sentence says nine).
